specAnchors.text: be able to describe the formation of ions in terms of loss or gain of electrons
be able to write ionic half-equations and use them to construct full ionic equations
be able to write formulae given oxidation numbers

primer.text: Full equations hide the ion that actually reacts. Ionic equations strip the spectators away, and half equations expose each electron transfer separately. This note builds ions from metals and non-metals, names compounds from oxidation numbers, then assembles the manganate-iron(II) equation step by step until the electrons cancel perfectly.

modules.title: Naming from oxidation numbers, ions from electrons
modules.opening: Oxidation numbers do double duty: they name compounds with variable-state metals and they track ion formation. This lesson names five transition-metal compounds from their states, then follows metals and non-metals as they shed or capture electrons.
keyPoints: Roman numerals from oxidation numbers distinguish copper(I) oxide from copper(II) salts.
Potassium manganate(VII) carries Mn at +7 and sodium dichromate(VI) carries Cr at +6.
Metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so they are oxidised and their number rises.
Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so they are reduced and their number falls.
Sodium in water climbs 0 to +1, while oxygen reacting with sodium falls 0 to -2.

low.restatement: Read the ion charges, solve the variable metal's state, name with Roman numerals; then sort the reactants - metals donate electrons and climb, non-metals accept and fall.
low.analogy: The oxidation number is a name tag printed at the door: compounds get labelled by their metal's tag, and the tag moves up or down exactly as electrons are handed over or taken in.
low.examPointer: In naming items, charge-balance first - Cu2O's two coppers must absorb the single oxide's -2, so each copper reads +1.

medium.restatement: Ion arithmetic resolves Stock names: Na2Cr2O7's two sodiums give +2, so the dichromate reads -2 and each chromium averages +6; the same arithmetic tracks cation and anion formation, where electron counts shift by whole numbers per atom.
medium.analogy: Splitting a restaurant bill: the fixed charges (oxide -2, sulfate -2) are known, and the variable metal's share is solved so the whole table settles to the observed total.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish chromate(VI) from dichromate(VI) by the 'di' prefix on the anion - both carry Cr at +6, but the ion formulas differ.

modules.title: Half equations and the dichromate build
modules.opening: Half equations isolate each electron transfer; the four-step routine handles the complicated ones. This lesson builds the dichromate-iron(II) ionic equation from two halves, multiplying until every electron cancels.
keyPoints: Half equations show only one half of an electron transfer: one species gaining or losing electrons.
Simple halves read directly, like Pb2+ + 2e- -> Pb or 2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-.
Oxygen-bearing ions need the four steps: balance the key atom, add H2O, add H+, add e-.
Multiplying the iron half by 6 lets the electrons cancel into the full ionic equation.

low.restatement: Write each half separately, then scale them until the electron counts match, add everything together, and the electrons vanish into a clean ionic equation.
low.analogy: Two shopping lists paid in one currency: multiply quantities until both lists cost the same number of coins, then merge - the coins (electrons) net out.
low.examPointer: Electrons must NEVER appear in the final ionic equation - a leftover e- means the halves were scaled wrongly.

medium.restatement: The four-step routine enforces atom, then oxygen (via water), then hydrogen (via H+), then charge (via e-) balance; matching the 6-electron reduction to six 1-electron oxidations aligns the ledger before cancellation.
medium.analogy: Tuning two engines to the same gear ratio: one turns 6 slow units, the other 6 fast ones, and the coupling cancels the mismatch.
medium.examPointer: Verify the dichromate half by charge arithmetic: the left side -2 + 14 - 6 = +6 and the right side 2 x (+3) = +6, so the half balances exactly.

modules.title: Balancing the manganate-iron equation directly
modules.opening: Oxidation numbers alone can balance a full ionic equation without writing the halves. This lesson runs the five-step direct method on MnO4- versus Fe2+, where manganese falls 5 units and iron climbs 1, and the coefficients fall out of the ledger.
keyPoints: Step 1 writes the unbalanced equation and flags the changing atoms: Mn and Fe.
Step 2 deduces the changes: Mn falls +7 to +2 and Fe rises +2 to +3.
Step 3 scales the ledger: one 5-unit fall needs five 1-unit climbs.
Step 4 balances charge with 8 H+ on the left, and step 5 balances atoms with 4 H2O.
The finished ionic equation is MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O.

low.restatement: Spot who changes, count the units each way, scale to equalise, then patch with H+ and water until charges and atoms agree.
low.analogy: Weighing two baskets on a balance: add iron coins (1 unit each) until they match the single manganese weight (5 units), then pour in acid and water until the whole scale settles.
low.examPointer: The 1:5 ratio of MnO4- to Fe2+ is the exam's favourite quotient - derive it from the 5-unit fall, never from memory alone.

medium.restatement: The ledger sets 1 MnO4- per 5 Fe2+; charge arithmetic then demands 8 H+, with the left side -1 + 10 + 8 = +17 matching the right side +2 + 15 = +17, and 4 H2O closes oxygen and hydrogen together.
medium.analogy: A three-column spreadsheet - atoms, charge, electrons - where fixing two columns forces the third; the ledger fixes columns two and three at once.
medium.examPointer: Show the charge arithmetic line explicitly: -1 + 10 + 8 = +2 + 15 = +17 - the verification earns the method marks.

glossary.definition: An equation showing one leg of an electron transfer, with electrons written explicitly on the gaining or losing side.
An equation showing only the reacting ions, with spectator species omitted.
An ion present in the mixture that takes no part in the electron transfer and is omitted from ionic equations.

workedExample.prompt: Use the oxidation-number ledger to write the overall redox equation for manganate(VII) ions oxidising iron(II) ions in acid.
steps: Step 1 - skeleton: MnO4- + Fe2+ -> Mn2+ + Fe3+, flagging Mn and Fe as the changing atoms.
Step 2 - deduce changes: Mn falls +7 to +2 (5 units); Fe rises +2 to +3 (1 unit).
Step 3 - balance the ledger: one 5-unit fall needs five 1-unit climbs, so 5Fe2+ per MnO4-.
Step 4 - balance charge with 8H+ on the left: -1 + 10 + 8 = +17 matches +2 + 15 = +17.
Step 5 - balance atoms with 4H2O: the ion's 4 oxygens and the 8 hydrogens close, giving MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O.
